title: Distinguishability Transitions from Global Quantum Snapshots
authors: Catherine McCarthy, Sarang Gopalakrishnan, Romain Vasseur
abstract: Quantum states generated by generic time evolution are locally featureless: local measurements return random outcomes that are identical for all states. However, global snapshots in the computational basis are surprisingly effective at distinguishing between quantum states. We explore the ability of Bayesian classifiers to discriminate between many random quantum states using a small number of measurement outcomes. We identify a phase transition in the ability of the classifier to distinguish between $k$ candidate states with $m$ shots controlled by the variable $x = m / \ln k$, and derive the threshold value $x_c$. We extend our results to low-depth circuits near the onset of anti-concentration, as well as to noisy circuits and phase-random states.
summary: This work analyzes how effectively one can distinguish between many random quantum states using limited global measurements. It establishes a precise phase transition governed by the ratio of shots to the logarithm of the number of states. The findings reveal that global measurements are surprisingly powerful, setting fundamental limits on quantum state distinguishability.
main_problem: The paper investigates the fundamental limits on distinguishing between a large number of random quantum states using only a small number of global measurement outcomes.
main_result: A phase transition is identified in the distinguishability, controlled by the ratio $x = m/\ln k$, with a critical threshold $x_c = 1/(1-\gamma)$.
method: The analysis employs Bayesian classification theory, calculating the success probability $P_s$ by analyzing the exponential decay of the misclassification probability in the large-shot limit.
model_or_system: The model involves $k$ candidate quantum states, $|\psi_\alphaangle$, assumed to be Haar-random or generated by random quantum circuits. Measurements are restricted to the computational basis, yielding global snapshots.
key_observables: Success probability ($P_s$) of the Bayesian decoder, and the critical scaling variable $x = m/\ln k$.
important_parameters: Number of states ($k$), number of shots ($m$), and the effective ratio $x = m/\ln k$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the availability of a classical model to compute the Born probabilities $p(\vec{m}|\psi_\alpha)$ for the decoder. Specific results rely on the Haar-random state assumption or the structure of Clifford circuits.

paper_structure: The paper first establishes the general framework using Bayesian classifiers for distinguishing random states, deriving the critical scaling $m \sim \ln k$. It then extends this analysis to specific physical regimes, including low-depth, noisy, and phase-random circuits, deriving specific limiting values like $2/3$ for Clifford circuits.
why_interesting: The concept of distinguishing quantum states via global measurements touches upon fundamental resource theories and information capacity, which has implications for quantum characterization and quantum metrology.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Left: Protocol for distinguishing k random states with m global snapshots. In this setup, an observer is presented with m copies of a random state |ψα⟩with α ∈{0, . . . , k −1} and provided with exact knowledge of all k states. After measuring each site of each of the m copies in the computational basis to obtain a set of bitstrings {⃗mi}, the observer queries a decoder in order to guess the label α. Here we take the decoder to be an optimal Bayesian classifier that outputs the label α associated with the largest probability p({⃗mi}|ψα), where p({⃗mi}|ψj) is computed for all j ∈{0, . . . , k −1} from the Born probabilities associated with the bitstrings {⃗mi}. Right: Decoder success...

FIG. 3. Top: onset of anti-concentration in finite-depth Clifford circuits. The decoder success probability Ps(t, N) decays from one to the expected value for random Clifford circuits Ps(t →∞, N) = 2/3 as the depth t of the circuit is increased. The curves for different system sizes collapse neatly when rescaling by t/ ln(N), indicating that anti-concentration sets in on logarithmic timescales. Bottom: The success prob- ability of an RMPO displays z/η scaling with η the rescaled noise strength in the small-z (deep) limit, and is indepen- dent of η in the large-z (shallow) limit (inset). The scaling in these two regimes is consistent with behavior seen in the linear XEB.
